title: State v. Roberts
description: Whether the state's failure to appoint counsel for an eligible criminal defendant for an extended period violates the right to counsel under Article I, section 11 of the Oregon Constitution, and if so, whether dismissal of the criminal case without prejudice is an appropriate remedy.
plaintiff_argument: The state argued that the failure to appoint counsel does not violate the right to counsel unless it causes 'incurable prejudice' to the defendant, and dismissal is only required in such instances.
defendant_argument: The relator (defendant) argued that the state's complete and indefinite denial of counsel for months, while criminal charges remained pending and he was subject to liberty restraints, violated his right to counsel, and dismissal without prejudice after a certain period (e.g., 30 days) was the only constitutionally adequate remedy.
decision_outcome: The court dismissed the alternative writ of mandamus as moot because the trial court had already dismissed the criminal case. However, the Supreme Court exercised its discretion to adjudicate the underlying constitutional questions, concluding that the state violated the relator's right to counsel and that dismissal without prejudice is required when counsel is not provided for more than 60 consecutive days in a misdemeanor case or 90 consecutive days in a felony case.

title: State v. Hemion
description: Whether the Washington County Circuit Court's order requiring Metropolitan Public Defender, Inc. (MPD) to disclose records regarding cases handled for its indigent clients was valid, with MPD arguing the legal bases were insufficient and the State of Oregon agreeing.
plaintiff_argument: Metropolitan Public Defender, Inc. (MPD) argued that the trial court's order, based on Article I, section 10, of the Oregon Constitution and the Public Records Law, was legally unsupported and erroneous.
defendant_argument: The State of Oregon (Adverse Party) agreed with MPD's argument that the trial court's legal bases for the order were erroneous and did not support the disclosure requirement.
decision_outcome: The court issued a peremptory writ of mandamus, directing the Washington County Circuit Court to vacate its order requiring Metropolitan Public Defender, Inc. to disclose records.

title: Scott-Schwalbach v. Rosenblum
description: Whether the Attorney General's certified ballot title for Initiative Petition 5 (IP 5) adequately describes the proposed measure in compliance with statutory requirements.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioner argued that the Attorney General's ballot title, specifically the caption, "yes" result statement, and summary, failed to adequately describe the measure's major effects, such as the elimination of school district discretion and the fiscal impact of funding following the student.
defendant_argument: The Attorney General argued that the ballot title substantially complied with statutory requirements, asserting that the "core legal effect" was the new parental right, not the removal of school district discretion, and that the summary appropriately omitted school funding impacts as they were not a "direct effect."
decision_outcome: The court concluded that the caption, the "yes" result statement, and the summary of the certified ballot title for IP 5 all required modification.

title: Arnold v. Kotek
description: Whether Ballot Measure 114, which requires a permit to purchase a firearm, completion of a background check at the point-of-transfer, and limits lawful firearm magazine capacity to 10 or fewer rounds, is facially constitutional under Article I, section 27, of the Oregon Constitution, with plaintiffs arguing it unduly burdens the right to bear arms for self-defense and defendants arguing it is a reasonable regulation to promote public safety.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Measure 114 was facially unconstitutional, asserting that the permit-to-purchase program created undue burdens and delays, and that the large-capacity magazine ban effectively banned most firearms and did not enhance public safety.
defendant_argument: The defendants (the State) argued that Measure 114 is facially constitutional under Article I, section 27, as it represents a reasonable legislative response to identifiable public safety threats and does not unduly frustrate the right to armed self-defense.
decision_outcome: The Court of Appeals reversed the circuit court's judgment, holding that all of Ballot Measure 114 is facially valid under Article I, section 27, and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

title: State v. Gonzalez
description: Whether a 90-month mandatory minimum sentence for first-degree arson violates the proportionality clause of Article I, section 16, of the Oregon Constitution, which requires all penalties to be proportioned to the offense.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the mandatory 90-month prison sentence for first-degree arson was constitutional and that the trial court erred by relying on the defendant's personal characteristics and circumstances in its proportionality analysis to reduce the sentence.
defendant_argument: Gonzalez argued that the 90-month mandatory minimum sentence was unconstitutionally disproportionate as applied to her, contending that her mental health issues and other mitigating circumstances should be considered to reduce her culpability, similar to how intellectual disability is considered.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the decision of the Court of Appeals, ruling that the 90-month mandatory minimum sentence for first-degree arson was not unconstitutionally disproportionate as applied to the defendant, thereby upholding the mandatory sentence.

title: State v. Dodge
description: Whether the Court of Appeals erred in ruling that the defendant failed to preserve his double jeopardy argument, which contended that retrying him on certain counts after a prior acquittal on similar, undifferentiated charges violated his constitutional rights.
plaintiff_argument: The state argued that the defendant's appellate argument on double jeopardy was not preserved because it differed from his trial argument, and that retrying the defendant on counts where he was previously convicted (and those convictions were reversed) constituted a "continuing prosecution" not barred by double jeopardy.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that retrying him on the six counts violated his double jeopardy rights because the lack of specificity in the indictment and first trial made it impossible to determine which incidents led to acquittals, creating a risk of conviction for acts he was already acquitted of.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, ruling that the defendant had adequately preserved his double jeopardy argument, and remanded the case for the Court of Appeals to address the merits of that argument.

title: Huskey v. Oregon Department of Corrections
description: Whether, in a civil action where the plaintiff alleges economic damages in the form of future lost employment income, the plaintiff must plead an "enforceable right" to that future employment to survive a motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim, with the plaintiff arguing no such right is required and the defendant arguing such a right is necessary.
plaintiff_argument: Plaintiff argued that he had properly pleaded economic damages for lost income and future impairment of earning capacity, and that Article I, section 41(3) of the Oregon Constitution did not require dismissal of his breach of contract claim, even if it denied him a right to employment.
defendant_argument: Defendant argued that Article I, section 41(3) of the Oregon Constitution, which states that "no inmate has a legally enforceable right to a job or to otherwise participate in work," rendered the plaintiff unable to plead economic damages because he had no right to employment.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision regarding the dismissal of the plaintiff's complaint for economic damages, holding that a lack of a "right" to future employment is not fatal to a claim alleging economic damages based on future earnings, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: State v. Autele
description: Whether a trial court's discretionary decision to deny a defendant's request to be represented by retained counsel of their choice may be affirmed on appeal only if the record created by the trial court establishes that its exercise of discretion was permissible.
plaintiff_argument: The state argued that the defendant failed to make an adequate record for appellate review, or alternatively, that the trial court properly denied the request for retained counsel due to a significant ethical conflict.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the trial court erred by denying his choice of retained counsel without an adequate record demonstrating a valid ethical conflict or risk of delay/disruption.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision and the circuit court's judgment, remanding the case for a new trial because the record did not adequately justify the denial of the defendant's right to retained counsel of choice.

title: Brown v. Kotek
description: Whether Governor Kotek had the authority to revoke Terri Lee Brown's conditional commutation after her sentence had expired, and whether Brown waived her right to challenge this revocation.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that Governor Kotek lacked the authority to revoke her conditional commutation after her sentence had expired, and that her purported waiver of rights was invalid or unenforceable.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that Governor Kotek had the authority to revoke the commutation even after the sentence expired, and that the plaintiff had validly waived her right to challenge the revocation.
decision_outcome: The court concluded that Governor Kotek lacked the authority to revoke the plaintiff's conditional commutation because her sentence had expired, and therefore ordered the plaintiff's immediate discharge from custody.

title: Thompson v. Fhuere
description: Whether the post-conviction court erred by modifying the petitioner's death sentence to life without the possibility of parole instead of remanding for resentencing, given the Governor's commutation and the procedural status of other claims.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that his death sentence and the penalty-phase questions were unconstitutional, requiring a remand for resentencing, and that the Governor's commutation did not preclude this relief.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the Governor's commutation rendered the issue moot, and the post-conviction court correctly modified the sentence to life without parole, with the penalty-phase claims being procedurally barred.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the post-conviction court's judgment, upholding the modification of the death sentence to life without parole and ruling that the penalty-phase claims were procedurally barred.

title: Knopp v. Griffin-Valade
description: Whether the disqualification for legislators with 10 or more unexcused absences applies to the immediate next term of office or the term after that.
plaintiff_argument: The disqualification should apply one term later, meaning a legislator would serve the next term but be disqualified for the term after that.
defendant_argument: The disqualification applies to the immediate next term of office following the term in which the absences occurred.
decision_outcome: The court upheld the Secretary of State's Temporary Rules ELECT 12-2023 and ELECT 16-2023, which apply the disqualification to the immediate next term of office.

title: State v. Wilcox
description: Whether the warrantless seizure of a defendant's backpack, during a non-criminal public intoxication custody, was lawful under Article I, section 9, of the Oregon Constitution, and if the Court of Appeals erred by applying a criminal seizure framework instead of an administrative one.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the backpack was not seized, or if it was, it was a lawful administrative seizure, and that the Court of Appeals erred by applying a criminal seizure framework to a non-criminal administrative seizure.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the Court of Appeals' seizure analysis was correct, finding the warrantless seizure unlawful under Article I, section 9, and that the Edwards precedent was controlling.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the decision of the Court of Appeals and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion, clarifying that the seizure should be analyzed under an administrative framework.

title: State v. Reed
description: Whether police officers violated Article I, section 12, of the Oregon Constitution by interrogating the defendant in compelling circumstances without first advising her of her Miranda rights, with the plaintiff arguing that the circumstances were not compelling and the defendant arguing that they were.
plaintiff_argument: The State of Oregon argued that the interrogation did not occur in compelling circumstances, therefore Miranda warnings were not required, and the evidence should not be suppressed.
defendant_argument: Deborah Lynn Reed argued that the interrogation occurred in compelling circumstances, violating her constitutional rights because she was not advised of her Miranda rights, and therefore the evidence should be suppressed.
decision_outcome: The Oregon Supreme Court reversed the decision of the Court of Appeals and the judgments of the circuit court, remanding the cases for further proceedings, ruling that the interrogation occurred in compelling circumstances and the evidence must be suppressed.

title: State v. Benton
description: Whether a private citizen, Layman, became a state agent for purposes of Article I, section 11, of the Oregon Constitution, with the State arguing he never was an agent and the Defendant arguing he was an agent from the beginning.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Layman was never acting as a state agent when questioning the defendant, and therefore all of Layman's testimony was admissible.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that Layman was acting as a state agent from the beginning of his interactions, and therefore none of Layman's testimony should be admissible.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, ruling that Layman became a state agent after his second proffer meeting on July 2, 2015, and therefore the defendant's statements made after that date should have been excluded, reversing and remanding convictions on Counts 1, 2, 6, and 7.

title: State ex rel Rosenblum v. Living Essentials, LLC
description: Whether the Unlawful Trade Practices Act (UTPA) provisions ORS 646.608(1)(b) and (1)(e) contain an implicit requirement that defendants' acts were "material to consumer purchasing decisions."
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, the State of Oregon, argued that the UTPA provisions do not require proof that misrepresentations were "material to consumer purchasing decisions" and that the lower courts erred in adding this implicit requirement.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the UTPA provisions implicitly require proof of materiality to consumer purchasing decisions and that without such a requirement, the provisions facially violate free speech protections under the state and federal constitutions.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the decision of the Court of Appeals, concluding that the UTPA provisions at issue do not contain a "material to consumer purchasing decisions" requirement and are not facially unconstitutional, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: State v. Craigen
description: Whether evidence obtained from questioning a represented defendant about charged crimes, without counsel present, must be suppressed in a separate murder trial.
plaintiff_argument: The state argued that the questioning was about an uncharged murder, for which the right to counsel had not attached, and even if there was a violation regarding the charged FIP crimes, the evidence should not be suppressed in the murder case.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the detectives violated his Article I, section 11 right to counsel by questioning him about the charged FIP crimes without his attorney present, and all evidence obtained from this violation must be suppressed in the murder trial.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, which held that the trial court erred in denying the defendant's motion to suppress evidence, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: State v. Colgrove
description: Whether ORS 138.105(5) precludes a defendant who has pleaded guilty or no contest from obtaining appellate review of legal challenges to the conviction in the judgment entered in the trial court, with the plaintiff arguing for a narrow reading that allows such review and the defendant arguing for a broad reading that precludes it.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that ORS 138.105(5) should be interpreted narrowly, meaning 'conviction' refers to a 'finding of guilt,' which would allow appellate review of legal challenges to the judgment of conviction, including the erroneous termination of a diversion agreement.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that ORS 138.105(5) broadly precludes appellate review of legal challenges to a conviction based on a guilty or no contest plea, and that 'conviction' refers to the judicial determination of guilt reflected in the judgment entered in the trial court.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, concluding that ORS 138.105(5) precludes appellate review of legal challenges to the conviction in the judgment entered in the trial court when a defendant pleads guilty or no contest, but reversed the circuit court's judgment for the costs of appointed counsel and vacated the DUII conviction fee.

title: State v. Ralston
description: Whether Christopher Shane Ralston's constitutional right to a speedy trial was violated due to delays in his felony DUII case and the subsequent loss of booking video evidence, with the defendant arguing prejudice from the lost video and the state arguing insufficient proof of prejudice.
plaintiff_argument: The state argued that the delays were largely explained and reasonable, and that the defendant failed to demonstrate a reasonable possibility of prejudice from the lost booking video to warrant dismissal of the charges.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the unexplained delays, particularly the six-week period leading to the loss of the booking video, violated his speedy trial rights and prejudiced his defense by depriving him of potentially exculpatory evidence.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, which affirmed in part and reversed in part the circuit court's judgment, concluding that the defendant had not met his burden to show prejudice from the delay, and thus his speedy trial rights were not violated.

title: State v. Thompson
description: Whether the five-day warrantless retention of a cell phone by police was an unlawful seizure under the Oregon Constitution, and if so, whether the admission of derivative evidence from the phone prejudiced the defendant.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the five-day warrantless retention of his cell phone was an unlawful seizure, and that evidence derived from it, including certain interview statements, should have been suppressed as prejudicial.
defendant_argument: The defendant (State) argued that the initial seizure and five-day retention of the phone were lawful due to probable cause and exigent circumstances, and that any error in admitting evidence was harmless.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the defendant's conviction, concluding that while the five-day retention of the phone was unlawful and the trial court erred in denying the motion to suppress, the error was harmless.

title: State v. Gray
description: Whether Article I, section 11, of the Oregon Constitution entitles a defendant to have counsel present in the grand jury room during their testimony, with the defendant arguing it is a critical stage of prosecution requiring counsel, and the state arguing that grand jury proceedings are closed and the statute does not create such a right.
plaintiff_argument: The state argued that grand jury proceedings are closed by statute to all but designated persons, not including a witness's attorney, and that the legislature did not intend to create a statutory or constitutional right to counsel's presence in the grand jury room.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that his voluntary appearance before the grand jury is a 'critical stage' of the prosecution, triggering his state constitutional right to have counsel present in the grand jury room during his testimony.
decision_outcome: The court concluded that a defendant has a state constitutional right to have counsel present in the grand jury room for consultation during their grand jury testimony, and issued a peremptory writ.

title: State ex rel. Kristof v. Fagan
description: Whether Nicholas Kristof met the durational residency requirement to be eligible for the office of Governor, which hinges on the interpretation of "resident within this State" as either a loose standard allowing dual residency or the legal concept of "domicile" requiring a single, fixed habitation with intent to remain permanently.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued for a looser standard of "resident" as someone intending to be at home in Oregon and acting on that intent, which would allow for residency in two states simultaneously. He also challenged the constitutionality of the durational residency requirement under the Equal Protection Clause.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that "resident within this State" refers to the legal concept of "domicile," which requires a fixed habitation with the intention to remain permanently or indefinitely, allowing a person to have only one domicile at a time. The defendant also contended that the durational residency requirement is not subject to strict scrutiny.
decision_outcome: The court dismissed the alternative writ of mandamus and denied the relator's petition, concluding that the Secretary of State was not compelled to find that the relator satisfied the durational residency requirement based on the legal definition of "domicile."

title: Whitehead v. Fagan
description: Whether the Secretary of State is required to count the signatures on an initiative petition of voters whose registration is deemed "inactive".
plaintiff_argument: Plaintiffs argued that voters with inactive registration are still registered and therefore remain "qualified voters" within the meaning of Article IV, section 1, and their signatures should be counted.
defendant_argument: The Secretary of State argued that voters with inactive registration are not "registered in the manner provided by law" and thus are not "qualified voters" within the meaning of Article IV, section 1, and their signatures should not be counted.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that voters whose registrations are inactive are not eligible to vote and therefore are not "qualified voters" within the meaning of Article IV, section 1, affirming the Secretary of State's exclusion of their signatures.

title: State v. McCarthy
description: Whether a warrantless search of a vehicle under the "automobile exception" requires actual exigent circumstances or if a per se exigency rule applies.
plaintiff_argument: The state argued that the warrantless search was justified under the "automobile exception" as established in State v. Brown, which allows for a per se exigency rule if the vehicle was mobile when stopped and there was probable cause.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the warrantless search violated Article I, section 9, of the Oregon Constitution and that the Brown per se exigency rule should be overruled, requiring actual exigent circumstances for a warrantless search.
decision_outcome: The court overruled the Brown per se exigency rule, holding that the state must prove actual exigent circumstances for a warrantless vehicle search, and affirmed the trial court's decision to suppress the evidence because the state failed to make that showing.

title: State v. Keys
description: Whether a defective waiver of a preliminary hearing deprives a circuit court of subject matter jurisdiction.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that a defective waiver of a preliminary hearing is a personal constitutional right, not a jurisdictional defect, and thus must be raised below or fall under a preservation rule exception.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that an invalid waiver of a preliminary hearing is a jurisdictional issue, meaning the circuit court lacks subject matter jurisdiction, and this issue can be raised for the first time on appeal, relying on Huffman.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Court of Appeals decision, holding that an invalid waiver of a preliminary hearing does not deprive a circuit court of subject matter jurisdiction, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: State ex rel. Kotek v. Fagan
description: Whether the Oregon Supreme Court has the authority to extend constitutional deadlines for legislative reapportionment, given the delay in federal census data, with plaintiffs arguing for extension and defendant arguing against it.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that due to the federal government's delayed release of 2020 census data, it is impossible to meet the constitutional deadlines for reapportionment, and requested the court to extend these deadlines and enjoin the Secretary of State from making a plan until the Legislative Assembly has had an opportunity to do so.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the court lacks the authority to extend the constitutional deadlines and that non-census data could be used to prepare an initial reapportionment plan, with any necessary revisions made during subsequent judicial review.
decision_outcome: The court allowed the relators' petition for a writ of mandamus, establishing revised deadlines for reapportionment, permitting the Legislative Assembly to enact a plan during an emergency session, and revising the residency timeline for candidates.

title: State v. Pittman
description: Whether compelling a criminal defendant to unlock a passcode-protected cell phone violates their right against self-incrimination under Article I, section 12, of the Oregon Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Compelling the defendant to unlock her phone and provide the passcode would violate her right against self-incrimination because it would provide incriminating, testimonial evidence that she owned or had access to the phone and its contents.
defendant_argument: Even if unlocking the phone is testimonial, its aspects are insignificant because the state already knows the facts (e.g., she possessed the phone and likely knew the passcode) and only seeks access to the phone's contents, not to learn new facts from her act.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, finding that the trial court's order compelling the defendant to unlock her cell phone violated her right against self-incrimination under Article I, section 12, of the Oregon Constitution because the state failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that it already knew the information the act would communicate and did not prohibit the use of the compelled act against the defendant.
